3rd-degree (complete) AV block.key: P waves and QRS complexes are each regular but completely independent (AV dissociation).
3rd-degree (complete) AV block.clue: The P waves march through at their own rate and the PR is never the same.

Wandering atrial pacemaker.key: Rate under 100 with at least 3 different P-wave shapes and a varying PR.
Wandering atrial pacemaker.clue: The P waves keep changing shape, but the rate stays below 100.

Junctional tachycardia.key: Junctional rhythm over 100; inverted P waves with a short PR (or none).
Junctional tachycardia.clue: Inverted P waves sit just before each QRS at a rate over 100.

Sinus rhythm with PACs.key: Sinus rhythm with an early beat whose P wave looks different; narrow QRS; non-compensatory pause.
Sinus rhythm with PACs.clue: Find the early beat and check that it has its own odd-shaped P wave.

Polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes).key: Wide rapid complexes that twist, growing and shrinking around the baseline.
Polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes).clue: The amplitude waxes and wanes, so the complexes seem to twist.

Normal sinus rhythm.key: Rate 60–100, regular, upright P before every QRS, PR 0.12–0.20 s, narrow QRS.
Normal sinus rhythm.clue: Everything is normal. Look for the problem in the patient, not the strip.

1st-degree AV block.key: Every P conducts, but the PR is > 0.20 s and constant.
1st-degree AV block.clue: The PR is long but never changes, and no beats drop.

Sinus tachycardia.key: Sinus rhythm at 100–150 with a visible upright P before each QRS.
Sinus tachycardia.clue: Visible upright P waves at under 150 point to sinus tachycardia, a response to something else.

Demand (VVI) pacing with native beats.key: Native beats, then paced beats appear only when the native rate drops.
Demand (VVI) pacing with native beats.clue: The pacer stays quiet until it's needed.

Accelerated junctional rhythm.key: Junctional rhythm at 60–100: narrow QRS, no normal P waves.
Accelerated junctional rhythm.clue: It's narrow and regular with no upright P, at a normal rate.

Ventricular paced rhythm.key: A pacer spike before each wide QRS, unrelated to P waves.
Ventricular paced rhythm.clue: One spike per beat, followed by a wide QRS.

Pacemaker failure to sense (undersensing.key: Spikes fire at a fixed rate regardless of native beats, landing on QRS or T waves.
Pacemaker failure to sense (undersensing.clue: The spikes ignore the patient's own beats.

Sinus rhythm with unifocal PVCs.key: Sinus rhythm with early, wide, bizarre beats of one shape and no P wave.
Sinus rhythm with unifocal PVCs.clue: The early wide beats all look the same.

P-wave asystole (ventricular standstill).key: P waves continue but no QRS complexes follow.
P-wave asystole (ventricular standstill).clue: The atria are firing, but there is no ventricular activity.

Junctional rhythm.key: Regular narrow QRS at 40–60; P waves absent, inverted before the QRS with a short PR, or inverted after it.
Junctional rhythm.clue: Narrow and 40–60, with no normal upright P waves.

AV sequential (dual-chamber) paced rhyth.key: Two spikes per beat: atrial spike → P, ventricular spike → wide QRS.
AV sequential (dual-chamber) paced rhyth.clue: Count the spikes: two per beat.

Pacer spikes without capture (asystole).key: Regular pacer spikes on an otherwise flat line: no capture at all.
Pacer spikes without capture (asystole).clue: Spikes but no P waves or QRS complexes, so this is an arrest.

Sinus rhythm with multifocal PVCs.key: PVCs of two or more different shapes.
Sinus rhythm with multifocal PVCs.clue: Compare the wide beats: they look different from each other.

Pacemaker failure to capture.key: Pacer spikes appear, but some are not followed by a P or QRS.
Pacemaker failure to capture.clue: Look for a spike with nothing after it.

Sinus bradycardia.key: Sinus rhythm (normal P, normal PR, narrow QRS) at a rate below 60.
Sinus bradycardia.clue: Every beat is a normal sinus beat. Only the rate is slow.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT).key: Rate over 100, irregular, with at least 3 different P-wave shapes and a varying PR.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT).clue: It's irregular like AF but has distinct P waves of changing shapes.

Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.key: Regular, wide, identical complexes over 100 (often 150–250); no P waves.
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.clue: Wide, fast and every complex the same.

Sinus rhythm with PJCs.key: Sinus rhythm with an early narrow beat that has an inverted P (short PR) or no P.
Sinus rhythm with PJCs.clue: The early beat is narrow, and its P wave is inverted or missing.

Atrial-sensed, ventricular paced rhythm.key: Native sinus P waves, each followed by a ventricular spike and wide QRS.
Atrial-sensed, ventricular paced rhythm.clue: The P waves are the patient's own and only the ventricle is paced.

Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).key: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150–250 with no visible P waves.
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).clue: Narrow, regular and fast, with the P waves hidden.

Sinus rhythm with a PVC couplet.key: Two PVCs in a row within a sinus rhythm.
Sinus rhythm with a PVC couplet.clue: Two consecutive wide beats. Three or more in a row is VT.

Atrial paced rhythm.key: A pacer spike before each P wave, then normal conduction with a narrow QRS.
Atrial paced rhythm.clue: The spike comes before the P wave, not before the QRS.

2nd-degree AV block type II (Mobitz II).key: Constant PR on conducted beats, then a P suddenly isn't conducted; QRS often wide.
2nd-degree AV block type II (Mobitz II).clue: The PR never changes before the dropped beat.

Pulseless electrical activity (PEA).key: An organized rhythm with no palpable pulse.
Pulseless electrical activity (PEA).clue: The strip looks organized, but the scenario says there is no pulse.

Atrial fibrillation.key: Irregularly irregular narrow QRS complexes with no P waves and a wavy fibrillatory baseline.
Atrial fibrillation.clue: No two R–R intervals match and there are no P waves.

Junctional bradycardia.key: Junctional rhythm (no normal P waves, narrow QRS) at a rate below 40.
Junctional bradycardia.clue: It looks junctional but is slower than the 40–60 escape rate.

2nd-degree AV block type I (Wenckebach).key: PR lengthens progressively until a P is not conducted; grouped beating.
2nd-degree AV block type I (Wenckebach).clue: The PR gets longer, longer, longer, then a beat drops.

Sinus rhythm with a junctional escape be.key: After a sinus pause, a late narrow beat appears with no normal P wave.
Sinus rhythm with a junctional escape be.clue: The odd beat comes LATE, after a pause, not early.

Transcutaneous pacing with capture.key: Large pacing artifacts, each followed by a wide QRS and broad T wave.
Transcutaneous pacing with capture.clue: Every artifact has a QRS and T after it, which is electrical capture.

Atrial flutter.key: Sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min; ventricular rate set by the conduction ratio.
Atrial flutter.clue: Look between the QRS complexes for the sawtooth baseline.

Sinus rhythm with ventricular bigeminy.key: Every other beat is a PVC: sinus, PVC, sinus, PVC.

2nd-degree AV block, 2:1.key: Every other P is conducted, with a constant PR on conducted beats.
2nd-degree AV block, 2:1.clue: Two P waves for every QRS, and the type can't be determined from 2:1 alone.

Ventricular fibrillation (fine).key: Low-amplitude chaotic undulation with no organized complexes.
Ventricular fibrillation (fine).clue: Small chaotic waves are still VF and still shockable. Asystole would be nearly flat.

Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR.key: Wide-QRS ventricular rhythm at 40–100 with no P waves.
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR.clue: It looks like idioventricular rhythm but faster. It's common after reperfusion.

Agonal rhythm.key: Very slow (< 20), very wide, low-amplitude complexes.
Agonal rhythm.clue: Broad, shapeless and very slow complexes are the signature of a dying heart.

Advanced (high-grade) AV block.key: Two or more consecutive P waves not conducted (3:1, 4:1); conducted beats have a constant PR.
Advanced (high-grade) AV block.clue: Several P waves in a row are blocked, yet each QRS still has a constant PR.

Sinus arrest (pause).key: Sinus rhythm interrupted by a pause that is NOT a multiple of the normal P–P interval.
Sinus arrest (pause).clue: Measure the pause: it doesn't fit a whole number of normal cycles.

Sinus arrhythmia.key: Identical sinus beats whose R–R interval speeds up and slows down in a smooth cycle.
Sinus arrhythmia.clue: The P waves never change. Only the spacing changes, gradually.

Pacemaker failure to pace (oversensing).key: A pause longer than the pacing interval with no spike.
Pacemaker failure to pace (oversensing).clue: There's a gap where a spike should be.

Transcutaneous pacing without capture.key: Large pacing artifacts not followed by a QRS; the underlying rhythm continues independently.
Transcutaneous pacing without capture.clue: The artifacts appear but the ventricles don't respond, so increase the mA.

Idioventricular rhythm.key: Regular wide QRS at 20–40, no P waves.
Idioventricular rhythm.clue: Wide and very slow with no P waves means the ventricles are pacing themselves.

Sinoatrial (SA) exit block.key: A dropped P–QRS–T where the pause is exactly two normal P–P intervals.
Sinoatrial (SA) exit block.clue: March out the P waves: the missing beat lands exactly where one was due.

Sinus rhythm with a run of VT (non-susta.key: Three or more consecutive PVCs at > 100/min, lasting under 30 seconds, then sinus resumes.
Sinus rhythm with a run of VT (non-susta.clue: A burst of wide beats starts and stops within the strip.

Ventricular fibrillation (coarse).key: Chaotic, irregular waves of varying size; no identifiable P, QRS or T.
Ventricular fibrillation (coarse).clue: No organized complexes at all, with large waves.

Sinus rhythm with ventricular trigeminy.key: Every third beat is a PVC: sinus, sinus, PVC.
Sinus rhythm with ventricular trigeminy.clue: Two normal beats, then one wide, repeating.

Asystole.key: No electrical activity: a nearly flat line.
Asystole.clue: No complexes and no P waves. Always confirm leads, gain and a second lead.

VT degenerating into VF.key: An organized wide tachycardia that breaks down into chaotic fibrillation.
VT degenerating into VF.clue: Compare the start and end of the strip: organized becomes chaotic.
